sentences.text: Falcarius was a primitive therizinosaurian theropod dinosaur that lived in North America during the Early Cretaceous period, serving as a transitional form between typical theropods and the more derived Therizinosauridae.

This animal resembles dinosaurs belonging to the Therizinosauridae subgroup within Maniraptora, yet it likely does not belong to that specific family but is part of the broader group Therizinosauria, which is characterized by wider hips, a large braincase, and long necks typical of plant-eaters.
Falcarius shared derived traits with therizinosaurids, including a long neck, a small head with plant-eating teeth, a robust arm with large claws, and a vertical body posture.

The name Falcarius means "sickle cutter" in Latin, referring to the animal's large hand claws, while its skull was small and elongated, supported by a very long neck made of elongated cervical vertebrae.

Falcarius retained a relatively long tail, and its forelimbs were not particularly long but showed signs of increasing robustness, with exceptionally thick epicondyles of the humerus indicating strong arm musculature. The foot bore weight on three toes.
It is assumed that Falcarius was covered in quill-like feathers, similar to less basal Asian therizinosaur specimens.
The smallest Falcarius specimens were under 1 meter long, while average adults reached 4 to 5 meters in length and weighed about 100 kilograms.
Falcarius could reach approximately 1.5 meters off the ground with its long neck to eat leaves or fruit.

Falcarius remains were first collected in the Cedar Mountain Formation in 1999, with more findings occurring in the 2000s, after collector Lawrence Walker discovered the fossils at the Crystal Geyser Quarry in Grand County.

The genus Falcarius contains two species, and the type species Falcarius utahensis was formally named in 2005 when a paper was published in the May issue of the journal Nature by Kirkland and colleagues.

A second site known as Suarez Quarry was reported in 2008, containing mainly adult individuals of a perhaps slightly different type, while two extensive bone beds were discovered containing the remains of hundreds, perhaps thousands, of Falcarius individuals. By 2010, the number of Falcarius specimens from the original quarry had risen to over 2,700, and later that year exceeded three thousand.

In 2010, Geminiraptor suarezarum was described as a new troodontid species based on an isolated maxilla from the Cedar Mountain Formation, while the holotype specimen of Falcarius, UMNH VP 15000, consists of a partial braincase with many paratypes assigned.
Falcarius had at least sixteen teeth in its upper jaw and twenty-eight teeth in the lower jaw, and it consumed plant material as indicated by its small, leaf-shaped, and finely serrated upper teeth.
The five longest, straighter, and more pointed teeth in the lower jaw suggest Falcarius might have had a partially omnivorous diet including small animals like lizards.
Smith published a study in 2026 analyzing the biomechanics of the forelimbs of Falcarius.
The genus Falcarius contains two species, and the species Falcarius suarezarum was originally placed in the distinct genus Geminiraptor in 2010.
Falcarius lived during the Berriasian to Valanginian stages, between 143.1 and 132.6 million years ago.

It is debated whether the species Falcarius suarezarum belongs to the troodontid genus Geminiraptor or to the therizinosaur genus Falcarius, as initial identification was based on a single jaw bone before later research suggested it was a therizinosaur similar to F. utahensis. A 2026 study by Freimuth, Lively, and Zanno reinterpreted the species "Geminiraptor" suarezarum as a member of Therizinosauria belonging to the genus Falcarius.
